headline: Cannabis-funded PAC backed 14 House Republicans; 13 lost seats
dek: A Trump-linked super PAC spent about $4 million of donations from Curaleaf, Trulieve, Verano and others on 14 House Republicans. Thirteen lost on 3 November.
key_points: America First Agriculture Action, a super PAC that shares a treasurer with Trump's MAGA Inc., spent about $3.96 million supporting 14 House Republicans in tough races, according to a tally of its filings by Marijuana Moment.
Thirteen of the 14 lost their seats in the 3 November midterms; the 14th race, in Alaska, was still uncalled when the tally was published on 13 November.

The money came largely from $11.5 million that Trulieve, Curaleaf, Verano, Ascend Wellness and entities tied to Green Thumb and AYR Wellness gave the PAC in June; the PAC's ads did not mention cannabis.
Several of the lawmakers backed had voted against federal legalization, and the bet bought the industry no friends in the next Congress, where Republican leaders remain opposed to reform.
body: Some of the largest US cannabis companies put millions of dollars into a Trump-linked super PAC this year, and the PAC spent much of it trying to save vulnerable House Republicans. It did not work. Of the 14 Republican members of Congress the PAC supported, 13 lost their seats in the 3 November midterm elections and one race, in Alaska, was still uncalled, according to a tally of the PAC's spending and the race results that Marijuana Moment published on 13 November.

The PAC is America First Agriculture Action Inc., a super PAC registered with the Federal Election Commission in May 2025. Its treasurer, Charles Gantt, is also treasurer of MAGA Inc., President Trump's main political committee. In June, Trulieve, Curaleaf, Verano, Ascend Wellness and entities tied to Green Thumb Industries and AYR Wellness gave it a combined $11.5 million, Marijuana Moment reported from FEC filings. None of the PAC's ads for the candidates mentioned cannabis.

The FEC's summary for the committee shows $13.75 million in total receipts and $11.98 million in total spending between its registration and 14 October 2026, including $4.01 million in independent expenditures, the category that covers ads and mail supporting or opposing a candidate. The FEC notes that its summary tables exclude the 24- and 48-hour reports filed close to an election, so late spending may not appear there yet.

Marijuana Moment's candidate-by-candidate tally shows the PAC's biggest single bet was Rep. Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, at about $529,000. Next came Rep. Nick Begich of Alaska (about $378,000), Rep. Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania (about $360,000), Rep. Tom Barrett of Michigan (about $359,000) and Rep. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona (about $356,000). Pennsylvania drew the most attention overall: four of the 14 incumbents backed, Bresnahan, Scott Perry, Ryan Mackenzie and Brian Fitzpatrick, represent the state.

Adding up the tally, MetaFlora counts about $3.96 million spent supporting the 14 Republicans, plus about $106,000 opposing Brian Poindexter, the Democrat who went on to beat Rep. Max Miller in Ohio. Roughly $3.58 million of the support went to the 13 who lost. Steil, Perry, Lawler, Fitzpatrick, Kiggans and the rest of the list are now out of Congress from January.
> The cannabis industry's biggest political bet of 2026 was spent on candidates who mostly opposed it, and it lost almost every race.

The spending drew criticism even before the votes were counted, because several of the Republicans it helped have records against cannabis reform. Fitzpatrick, Perry and Steil, the longest-serving members on the list, all voted against the Democratic-led bills to legalize marijuana federally that passed the House in 2020 and 2022, Marijuana Moment reported. Rep. Jen Kiggans voted against legalization as a Virginia state senator, and Mackenzie voted against Pennsylvania's medical cannabis law as a state lawmaker in 2016.

Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, who received about $289,000 in support, said in a September debate that legalization is hurting society, according to the same report. He has also argued that rescheduling would be wrong and is a cosponsor of a bill to keep the Section 280E tax penalty in place for marijuana businesses even after rescheduling. That position cuts directly against the tax relief the donating companies expect from the move to Schedule III.

The PAC's ads instead touted the incumbents' votes on other issues, such as a ban on congressional insider trading and tax cuts on tips and overtime. The companies' apparent aim was not to win cannabis votes from these members but to stay close to the administration that is carrying out rescheduling. Cannabis businesses and an industry-linked committee have given at least $15.05 million to Trump-linked PACs in total, Marijuana Moment found, and Trulieve and Curaleaf gave $1 million combined to the Trump inaugural committee after the 2024 election.
## What it means for the companies

For investors, the episode is a reminder that the US industry's federal gains this year came from the executive branch, not Congress. The Justice Department's rescheduling of medical marijuana and the DEA registrations that followed were administration actions. Congress, by contrast, has not passed SAFER Banking, and the GOP-controlled House Appropriations Committee voted this year to block further rescheduling work, though the Senate's version of the bill, as we reported on 13 November, leaves that freeze out.

The losses do not change those dynamics on their own. Republicans' new leaders in both chambers oppose reform, as we reported on 12 November, and the members the PAC tried to save were not cannabis champions to begin with. But the donors spent heavily in races that turned against their party's candidates, and they did so in a way that critics in the reform movement had already called self-defeating. Several of the companies named, including Curaleaf, Trulieve, Verano and Green Thumb, are publicly traded, and their shareholders have now seen eight-figure political spending with little to show for it in the House.

The companies themselves have not commented on the results in the reporting MetaFlora reviewed. Marijuana Moment noted that House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has separately raised funds from cannabis executives, a sign that the industry is spreading its bets.

The next FEC reports will show whether the PAC's late spending, filed in 24- and 48-hour reports, changes the totals, and how much of its $1.77 million in cash on hand at 14 October it spent before polling day. The Alaska race involving Begich is the last result to settle. In Congress, the lame-duck session must pass funding by 11 December, when the current stopgap expires and the second phase of the federal hemp ban is due; that bill will show whether the House's rescheduling freeze survives. From January, watch which members of the new Congress cannabis companies choose to back, and whether they keep routing money through Trump-aligned committees.
